poems.text: You are often wont to ask me what sort of person I should be, Priscus, if I became rich and were suddenly powerful. Do you think any man can declare his character in future .'' Tell me, if you became a lion, what sort of lion will you be?

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 93 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Labulla has discovered how to kiss her lover in the presence of her husband. She gives repeated kisses to her dwarf fool; this creature, slobbered with many kisses, the lover at once pounces upon, fills him up with his own kisses, and hands him back to the smiling lady. How much bigger as a fool is the husband!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 94 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I was writing an epic; you began to write one: left off, that my poems should not stand in rivalry with yours. My Thalia shifted to tragic buskins: you also fitted on yourself the long train of tragedy. I struck the strings of a lyre practised by the Calabrian Muses: you, ambitious man, snatch from me the new quill. I venture satire: you strain to be a Lucilius. I sport with light elegies: you, too, sport with the same thing. What lesser art can there he? I begin to model epigrams: in this quarter, too, my fame is already sought after by you. Pick out something you do not want — for what modesty is there in wanting everything? — and if there is anything you don't want, Tucca, leave it to me.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 98 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Baetis, with thy hair wreathed with the olive crown, that dippest thy golden fleeces in sparkling waters, whom Bromius, whom Pallas loves, to whom the king of waters, Albula, opens a path that wafts the ships over the seas, with glad omens may Instantius first tread thy shores, and this year pass for the peoples as the last. He is not blind to the burthen of succeeding Macer: he that gauges his load can bear it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 1 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That tunny-fry may not lack a gown, and olives a capote/ nor the foul black beetle fear pinching hunger, destroy, ye Muses — the loss is mine — papyrus from the Nile: see tipsy winter calls for new pleasantries, No die of mine contends with dauntless weapon, nor does sice together with ace shake my ivory box: this paper is my nuts, this paper is my dice-box; hazard that brings me no loss nor yet any gain.

poems.title: Book XIII, 2 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although you have always a critic's nose, are in a word a nose so great that Atlas on request would not have consented to shoulder it, and though you can deride even Latinus himself, you cannot say more against my trifling effusions than I have said myself. What pleasure is there in tooth gnawing tooth? you require flesh if you want to be fat. Lest you should waste your time, keep your venom for those that fancy themselves; I know these efforts of mine are nothing worth. And yet not altogether nothing if you come to me with a just ear, and not with a morning aspect.

poems.title: Book XIII, 3 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The whole collection of Mottoes in this slender little volume will cost you to buy four sesterces. Is four too much. it can cost you two, and bookseller Tryphon would make his profit. These distichs you can send to your guests instead of a gift, if a coin shall be as rare with you as with me. In addition you will get the names of the things on the headings: pass it by if anything is not to your stomach.

poems.title: Book XIII, 4: Incense (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That it may be late ere Germanicus rule the palace of Heaven, and that he may long rule earth, give pious incense to Jove.

poems.title: Book XIII, 5: Pepper (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When a beccafico, with its bright waxen flesh and plump sides, falls to you by lot, if you have taste, add pepper.

poems.title: Book XIII, 6 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I can send you barley-water, a rich man will be able to send you mead. If the rich man be unwilling to send it, you will buy.

poems.title: Book XIII, 7 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If pale beans bubble for you in a red earthenware pot you can often decline the dinners of sumptuous hosts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 8 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Flavour common jars with pulse from Clusium, that, after dinner, you may drink from them, when empty, new wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 9 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive lentils of Nile, a present from Pelusium; tliey are cheaper than spelt, dearer than beans.

poems.title: Book XIII, 10 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: One cannot enumerate the properties or the uses of flour, seeing that it is so often handy for the baker and the cook.

poems.title: Book XIII, 11 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive something for your muleteer to withhold from your mules that will not blab. I have given this to the inn-keeper, not to you, as a gift.

poems.title: Book XIII, 12: Com (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Take three hundred pecks from the harvest of the Libyan farmer, that your suburban land may not gi"ow sterile.

poems.title: Book XIII, 13 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That insipid beet the noon-meal of artizans, may acquire flavour, oh, how often will the cook ask for wine and pepper!

poems.title: Book XIII, 14 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Tell me, why is it that lettuce, which used to end our grandsires' dinners, ushers in our banquets?

poems.title: Book XIII, 15 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you till fields near to me at Nomentum, I remind you, rustic, to bring wood to my villa.

poems.title: Book XIII, 16 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These rapes, delighting in winter's cold, which I give you, in heaven Romulus is wont to eat.'

poems.title: Book XIII, 17 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In order that pale sprouts may not move your disgust, let the cabbage become green in water and soda.

poems.title: Book XIII, 18 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: As often as you have eaten the strong-smelling shoots of Tarentine leeks, give kisses with shut mouth.

poems.title: Book XIII, 19: Headed Leeks (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Woody Aricia sends the finest leeks: observe on the white stem the green blades.

poems.title: Book XIII, 20 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These the land of Amiternum nurtures in its fertile gardens; the round rapes of Nursia you will be able to eat at less cost.

poems.title: Book XIII, 21 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The succulent stalk that has grown in watery Ravenna will not be more palatable than wild asparagus.

poems.title: Book XIII, 22 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I am a grape unfit for the wine-cup and worthless to LyaeuSj but, if you do not drink me, I shall be nectar to you.

poems.title: Book XIII, 23: Chian Figs (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A Chian fig is like the old wine Setia has sent you; it carries in itself new wine, and in itself salt too.

poems.title: Book XIII, 25 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We are Cybele's apples "; depart far hence, traveller, lest our downfall descend on your wretched head.

poems.title: Book XIII, 26 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We are service berries that astrict too relaxed bowels; you will better give these apples to your boy than to yourself.

poems.title: Book XIII, 27 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A gilt date is offered on the kalends of January; but yet this is wont to be the gift of a poor man.

poems.title: Book XIII, 28: A Jar of small Syrian Figs (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These Syrian figs, which, stored in a round conical jar, have reached you, would, if largei-, be figs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 29 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Take plums wrinkled by shrivelling old age abroad: they are used to lighten the load of an obstinate stomach.

poems.title: Book XIII, 30 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Cheese, stamped with the crest of Etruscan Luna, will afford your slaves a thousand lunches.

poems.title: Book XIII, 31 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you wish without meat to take a frugal breakfast, this lump comes to you from a Vestinian flock.

poems.title: Book XIII, 32 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: It is not every heat, or every smoke that a cheese imbibes; but that which has imbibed V elabran has flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 33 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Trebula gave us birth; a double excellence recommends us; we are tamed by a moderate fire or by water.

poems.title: Book XIII, 34 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Since your wife is an old woman, and your members are nerveless, you can do nothing but satisfy your hunger with bulbs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 35 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Daughter of a Picenian sow, here I come, a Lucanian sausage; with me you may put a toothsome garnish round white pottage.

poems.title: Book XIII, 36: A Small Box of Olives (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These olives which have reached you, withdrawn from the oil presses of Picenum, begin and also end our repasts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 37 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These were either from the branches of Corcyra's garden, or they were apples, the Massylian dragon's charge.

poems.title: Book XIII, 38 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Beestings, whereof the shepherd has robbed the kids while not yet able to stand, I give you fi-om the first milk of the dams.

poems.title: Book XIII, 39: Kid (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let the wanton beast, and one of no service to the green vine, pay the penalty; though young, it has already injured the god.

poems.title: Book XIII, 40: Eggs (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If a white liquid surround the saffron-coloured yolks, let the sauce of Spanish mackerel season the eggs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 41 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let a rich man set before me the nursling, fed on milk alone, of a lazy mother, and let him eat of an Aetolian boar.

poems.title: Book XIII, 42 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I do not give you tuber-apples and pomegranates from Libyan boughs, but from my Nomentan trees.

poems.title: Book XIII, 43: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Culled from suburban boughs are sent you pomegranates and home-grown tuber-apples. What do you want with Libyans?

poems.title: Book XIII, 44: Sows Paps (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You would think it not yet a dish of udder, so full-flowing is the dug, and so does the pap swell with living milk.

poems.title: Book XIII, 45: Fonds (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If I possessed guinea-fowls and pheasants you should receive them; but now receive the birds of the farmyard.

poems.title: Book XIII, 46 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Of little worth should we peaches have been on the branches of our mother tree; now on adoptive boughs we peaches are prized.

poems.title: Book XIII, 47 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The bread of Picenum jrrows big with its white nectar as a light sponge swells when it has taken in water.

poems.title: Book XIII, 48: Mushrooms (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Silver and gold, and a mantle, and a toga it is easy to send; to send mushrooms is difficult.

poems.title: Book XIII, 49 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Seeing that figs nourish me, seeing that I am fed on sweet grapes, why did not the grape rather give me my name .''

poems.title: Book XIII, 50 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We truffles that burst through the nurturing soil with our soft heads are of earth's apples second to mushrooms.

poems.title: Book XIII, 51 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A circlet woven of roses or rich spikenard perhaps pleases you, but one made of fieldfares pleases me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 52 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: LI I. — Ducks Let a duck certainly be served up whole; but it is tasty only in the breast and neck: the rest return to the cook.

poems.title: Book XIII, 53: Turtle-doves (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When I shall have a fat turtle-dove, good-bye, lettuce; and keep the snails for yourself. I don't want to spoil my appetite.

poems.title: Book XIII, 54 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let me have Cerretanian gammon served to me, or it may be sent from the Menapians; let gourmets devour ham.

poems.title: Book XIII, 55: Ham (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: It is freshly cured: make haste, and do not put off your dear friends; for let me have nothing to do with an old ham.

poems.title: Book XIII, 56 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You perhaps the womb of a virgin pig may allure more: the maternal womb of a pregnant sow allures me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 57: Egyptian Beans (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You will scoff at this vegetable from Nile and its tenacious threads when with teeth and hands you draw out its stubborn fibres.

poems.title: Book XIII, 58 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: See how the liver is swollen bigger than a big goose! In wonder you will say: "Where, I ask, did this grow?"

poems.title: Book XIII, 59 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: All my winter is passed in sleep, and I am fatter at that season during which nothing but sleep nourishes me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 60 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A rabbit delights in dwelling in burrowed holes: he taught foes the art of secret paths.

poems.title: Book XIII, 61 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Of all flavours of fowls the most tasty is said to be that of Ionian heathcocks.

poems.title: Book XIII, 62 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The hen is easily fattened on sweetened meal; it fattens, too, on the dark. Ingenious is gluttony!

poems.title: Book XIII, 63 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That the cock might not grow thin by over indulgence, he has been gelded. Now he will be to me a Gaul.

poems.title: Book XIII, 64: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In vain the hen submits to her sterile husband. This bird it beseemed to have been the bird of Mother Cybele. LX V. — Partridges This bird is very rarely served on Italian tables: one often sees it playing in the fishpond.

poems.title: Book XIII, 65: Doves (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Do not violate with profane tooth tender doves, if the rites of the goddess of Cnidos have been entrusted to you.

poems.title: Book XIII, 67 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Ringdoves check and blunt the manly powers: let not him eat this bird who wishes to be lickerish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 68 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The green bird is beguiled by canes and nets at the season when the young grape is swelling with juice yet immature.

poems.title: Book XIII, 69 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Umbria has never supplied us with Pannonian cattae; these are the gifts Pudens prefers to send to his lord.

poems.title: Book XIII, 70 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Dost thou admire it, oft as it spreads its spangled wings, and hast the heart, unfeeling man, to deliver this bird to a cruel coo'li?

poems.title: Book XIII, 71 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: My ruddy wing gives me a name, but my tongue is a delicacy to gluttons. What if my tongue were to speak?

poems.title: Book XIII, 72 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I was transported first by Argo's keel; ere that Phasis was all I knew.

poems.title: Book XIII, 73 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although Hannibal ate his fill of Roman geese, yet the barbarian never ate the birds of his own land.

poems.title: Book XIII, 74 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This bird saved the Thunderer's Tarpeian fane. Do you wonder.'' a god had not yet built it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 75 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You will disorder the lines, and the letter will not fly complete if you make away with a single bird of Palamedes.

poems.title: Book XIII, 76 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Whether I am woodcock or partridge, what does it matter if the flavour be the same > A partridge is dearer. 'Tis thus it has better flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 77: Swans (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The swan gives forth its sweet measured song with failing tongue itself the minstrel of its own death.

poems.title: Book XIII, 78 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Has so small a bird the name of a great giant? [t has, too, the name of Porphyrion of the Green.

poems.title: Book XIII, 79 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The mullet breathes in the sea-water brought A'ith him, but, already torpid, he begins to languish. 3ive him the fresh sea; he will be strong.

poems.title: Book XIII, 80 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The big lamprey that swims in the Sicilian deep;ea has not the strength to plunge when its skin is jcorched by the sun.

poems.title: Book XIII, 81 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: However wide is the dish that bears the turbot, y et the turbot is wider than the dish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 82: Oysters (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Drunken with the water of Baiae's Lucrine,! have I, a shell-fish, just arrived. Now, luxurious that I am, I thirst for the noble pickle.

poems.title: Book XIII, 83 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Cerulean Liris, which Marica's wood guards, is fond of us: from hence we prawns come in greatest numbers.

poems.title: Book XIII, 84 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Of this sea-bream, which has come lean from the sea-waves, the entrails are good eating; as to the rest it has poor flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 87 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Cloaks dyed in our blood/ ingrate, you put on; and this is not enough: we are your food.

poems.title: Book XIII, 88 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In Venetian territory, however choice may be the entertainment, the beginning of the dinner is wont to be a gudgeon.

poems.title: Book XIII, 89 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Soft and white the bass breasts the mouths of Euganean Timavus, fed on fresh water and the salt of the sea.

poems.title: Book XIII, 90 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Not every gilthead deserves praise and a big price, but the one that feeds only on Lucrine shell-fish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 91 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Send sturgeon to Palatine tables; let rare offering adorn ambrosial feasts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 92: Hares (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Amongst birds the fieldfare, if my judgment can aught decide, amongst quadrupeds the primest delicacy is a hare.

poems.title: Book XIII, 93: Boar (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The terror in the land of Diomedes, the bristly beast that fell beneath an Aetolian spear/ was such as this.

poems.title: Book XIII, 94: Doe (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: For his tusk is the boar dreaded, his horns defend the stag; we, unwarlike does, what are we but a prey?

poems.title: Book XIII, 95 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Not the meanest quarry among the beasts of morning shows, the savage oryx costs me the death of how many dogs!

poems.title: Book XIII, 96: The Stag (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Was this the stag tamed by your halter, Cyparissus, or rather was it your stag, Silvia .''

poems.title: Book XIII, 97 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: While he is a young wild ass, and is fed by his mother alone, the lalisio has, as a nursling, this name, but one short-lived.

poems.title: Book XIII, 98 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You will see a roe "poised on the summit of a rock; one can only hope she will fall; she is showing contempt of the dogs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 99 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You shall give a gazelle as a pet to your little son. The crowd loves to procure its dismissal by fluttering their togas.

poems.title: Book XIII, 100: The Wild Ass (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A beautiful wild ass comes; the hunt of the Indian tusk must be sent away; now shake your togas no longer.

poems.title: Book XIII, 101 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This oil the berry of Campanian Venafrum has distilled for you; your unguent, as often as you use it, smells too of that oil.

poems.title: Book XIII, 102 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive this proud sauce, made of the first blood of a mackerel breathing still, an expensive gift.

poems.title: Book XIII, 103: A Jar of Tunny-fish Sauce (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Daughter of the tunny of Antipolis I confess I aui. Were I of the mackerel, I should not have been sent to you.'

poems.title: Book XIII, 104 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This the bee, spoiler of Thesean Hymettus, has sent you, noble nectar from the woods of Pallas.

poems.title: Book XIII, 105 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When you make a present of Sicilian combs from amid Hybla's hills ' you may say they are Attic combs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 106 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The vintage of Gnossos in Minoan Crete brought forth for you this, which is wont to be the poor man's mead.

poems.title: Book XIII, 107 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That this pitch -flavoured wine came from vine-bearing Vienna do not doubt; Romulus himself sent it to me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 108 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You, Attic honey, thicken the nectarous Falernian. It is meet that such a drink be mixed by a Ganymede.

poems.title: Book XIII, 109: Alban Wine (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This wine the mild grape, proud of itself on the Julian mount, sends you from Caesar's cellars.

poems.title: Book XIII, 110 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Drink you Surrentine .'' Take not beakers ot painted murrine, nor of gold: these wines will supply you with their native cups.

poems.title: Book XIII, 111: Falernian Wine (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: From presses of Sinuessa has the Massic come. Stored in what consul's year do you ask .'' there was no consul then.

poems.title: Book XIII, 112 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Setia high-poised, that looks on the Pomptine levels, has sent from a tiny city casks of aged wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 113 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This Fundanian the rich autumn of Opimius' year produced. The consul squeezed out the must, and himself drank the wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 114 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I am not, I confess, of the first brand of Lyaeus; yet among wines my vintage shall be the seventh.

poems.title: Book XIII, 115 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I Generous Caecuban is ripened at Amyclae by Fundi, and the vine grows green, born in the middle of the marsh.

poems.title: Book XIII, 116 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Paei.ignian wine-growers send you turbid Marsic,vine. Do not driuk it yourself, but let your freednan do so.

poems.title: Book XIII, 122: Vinegar (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let not a jar of Egyptian vinegar be mean in your syes. When it was wine it was more mean.

poems.title: Book XIII, 123 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When your dole shall strike off the list a hundred citizens, you can serve them the smoky wines of Massilia.

poems.title: Book XIII, 124 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let Nepos serve Caeretan, you will imagine it Setine. He does not serve it to a crowd: with three guests he drinks it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 125 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let Aulon, renowned for wool and blest in vines, give precious fleeces to you, wines "to me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 126: Unguent (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Unguent or wine never bequeath to your heir; let him have your cash: the whole of these give to your own self.

poems.title: Book XIII, 127: A Crown of Roses (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Forced coronals winter gives thee, Caesar: erewhile the rose was Spring's: now has it become thine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 1 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: While the knight and My Lord the Senator rejoice in dinner-dress, while wearing freedom's cap beseems our Jove, and the home-bred slave, as he shakes the dice-box, does not fear to look the Aedile in the face, when he sees the cold tanks so near, receive these lots, gifts of rich and poor alternate; let everyone give his own guest his proper prize. "They are worthless and gira-cracks, or anything still meanei", if possible." Who does not know it? Or who denies what is so plain? But what else am I to do, Saturn, on the unsober days your son himself gave you in exchange for Heaven? Do you wish me to write of Thebes, or Troy, or guilty Mycenae? "Play with nuts," you say. I don't want to lose my nuts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 2 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You can finish this little book at whatever point you like; every subject is summed up in two verses. If you ask why headings are added, I will explain: it is that, if you prefer, you may read the headings only.

poems.title: Book XIV, 3: Tablets of Citrus-wood (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Had not our wood been cut into thin plates, we should have been the noble burden of a Libyan tusk.

poems.title: Book XIV, 4: Five-leaved Tablets (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The glad court of our master is warm with the slaughter of steers, when by the five-leaved waxen tablet is conferred on him high honour.

poems.title: Book XIV, 5: Ivory Tablets (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Lest dark-coloured waxen tablets dim your failing eyesight, let black letters dye for you snow-white ivory.

poems.title: Book XIV, 6: Three-leaved Tablets (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You will then deem my three-leaved tablets no mean gift, when your mistress shall write to you that she will come.

poems.title: Book XIV, 7: Parchment Tablets (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Imagine these tablets are waxen, although they are calltd parchment. You will rub out as often as you wisli to write afresh."

poems.title: Book XIV, 8 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although she may not as yet have read them, a girl knows what Vitellian tablets wish for.

poems.title: Book XIV, 9: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Because you see we are very small, you believe we are being sent to a mistress. You are mistaken: a tablet of that sort also duns for money.

poems.title: Book XIV, 10 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: There is no reason you should think the offering puny when a poet gives you blank sheets.

poems.title: Book XIV, 11: Letter-paper (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Whether sent to a slight acquaintance or to a dear comrade, this paper is accustomed to address everyone as its "Dear friend."

poems.title: Book XIV, 12 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: To fill these money-boxes with anything but yellow money is unfitting: let cheap wood carry silver.

poems.title: Book XIV, 13 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If anything still remain at the bottom of me, a little money-box, it shall be a gift. Is there nothing.'' The little box itself shall be the gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 14: Ivory Knuckle-bones (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When no one of the bones you throw stands with the same face as another you will say I have given you a great present.

poems.title: Book XIV, 15 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let us dice be not equal in number to the knuckle-bones," if only our stakes be often greater than with the knuckle-bones.

poems.title: Book XIV, 16 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If the cheating hand, that knows how to arrange and throw the bones, has thrown them through me, he will achieve nothing beyond prayers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 17 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: On this side of rne dice ai-e counted by double sixes: on this other the piece of hostile colour is taken by twin foemen.

poems.title: Book XIV, 18 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Nuts appear a small stake, and one not ruinous; yet often has that stake made prize of boys' buttocks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 19 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Having won the case in the raffle, remember to equip it with pens: we have given you all else, do you provide the slighter things.

poems.title: Book XIV, 20: Draught Pieces (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you play the war-game of robbers in ambush, these glass pieces will be your soldiers and their enemies.

poems.title: Book XIV, 21: A Style-case (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This style-case, fitted with its proper iron styles, shall be for you: if you give it to your boy, it will be no slight gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 22 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Mastick is better; but if pointed wood be not forthcoming, a quill can relieve your teeth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 23 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If your ear is troubled with a persistent itching, I give you an instrument appropriate to such vagaries.

poems.title: Book XIV, 24 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That your moistened hair may not soil your bright silks, let a pin fix and hold up your knotted locks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 25: Combs (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: What will be the use, when it will find here no hair, of this many-toothed piece of box which is given you?

poems.title: Book XIV, 26 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The spume of the Chatti turns to flame Teutonic locks: you can be smarter with the hair of a captive slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 27 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If white-haired you are set on dyeing your aged locks, accept — why be hairless? — these balls from Mattiacum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 28 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Accept a sunshade to subdue the overpowering heat; even though there be a wind, your own awning will cover you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 29 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I will be a spectator with you in Ponipey's theatre for blasts of wind are apt to deny the people an awning.

poems.title: Book XIV, 30: Hunting-spears (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: They will counter boars, and will wait for the lion's rush; they will pierce bears if the hand be but firm enough.

poems.title: Book XIV, 31 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you lament that your hunting spear with its long blade has been struck down, this short weapon will closely engage a huge boar.

poems.title: Book XIV, 32 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A soldier's decoration is this, and it will be a sign of a prized honour, a weapon worthy to gird a tribune's side.

poems.title: Book XIV, 33 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This dagger, which a narrow circle marks with its rounded groove, Salo dipt while it was hissing in his chilling waters.

poems.title: Book XIV, 34: Sickle (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Me our Captain's assured peace has bent to serve quiet uses: the husbandman's am I now, the soldier's was I aforetime.

poems.title: Book XIV, 35: A Small Axe (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: When a melancholy auction for payment of debts was held, this was bought for four hundred thousand sesterces.

poems.title: Book XIV, 36 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These instruments are suitable for the cutting of your hair; this one is serviceable to long nails, that to your cheeks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 37 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Unless you provide me '' with choice books I will let in moths and savage bookworms.

poems.title: Book XIV, 38 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The land of Memphis supplies reeds handy for writing: let your roof be thatched with the reeds from other marshes.

poems.title: Book XIV, 39 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I am a lamp, privy to the pleasures of your couch: you may do what you will, I shall be silent.

poems.title: Book XIV, 40 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The lot has given you the lamp's handmaid, which is awake and dispels complete darkness.

poems.title: Book XIV, 41 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although I illume whole entertainments with my flames, and carry so many wicks, I am called a single lamp.

poems.title: Book XIV, 42 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This taper will afford you light by night, for your lamp has been stolen from your slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 43 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Candles gave me my name of old; the oil-lamp had no knowledge of our thrifty sires.

poems.title: Book XIV, 44 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You see I am wood; unless you guard the light, a great lamp will be made of your candelabrum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 45 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This ball which swells with tip;htly-crammed feathers is less flaccid than the bladder-ball and less compact than a hand-ball.

poems.title: Book XIV, 46 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you know how to bandy me with your nimble left-handers, I am yours. Don't you know how .'' You clown, give back the ball.

poems.title: Book XIV, 47 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Go far off, you young men; unstrenuous age befits me: with the bladder-ball it becomes boys to play, with the bladder-ball old men.

poems.title: Book XIV, 48 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These the dissolute youth, who with empty labour makes big his neck, swiftly catches at on the dusty ground of Antaeus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 49 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Why is strength of arm wasted on the silly dumb-bell.'' Trenching a vineyard better employs men.

poems.title: Book XIV, 50: A Small Cap (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That the wrestler's dirty oil may not soil your sleek locks, you may cover your moist hair with this skin cap.

poems.title: Book XIV, 51 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Pergamus sent these; scrape yourself with the curved blade: the laundryman will not so often wear out your towels.

poems.title: Book XIV, 52 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A steer bore me lately on his forehead: you fancied me a real rhinoceros horn.

poems.title: Book XIV, 53 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This shalTbe for you, that horn, lately seen in our Master's Italian arena, to which a bull was as a straw-dummy.

poems.title: Book XIV, 54 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If any little home-born slave shall hang on your neck in tears, let him shake this noisy rattle with his infant hand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 55: Whip (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You will make no way with this whip though you may continually use the lash, if your courser be of the Purple faction.

poems.title: Book XIV, 56 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: What have you to do with me.'' Let a young maid use me: I am not wont to polish purchased teeth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 57 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: ThiSj which neither Virgil nor Homer mentions in his poems/ is compounded of unguent and ben-nut.

poems.title: Book XIV, 58 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Are you a countryman? You do not know what I am styled by a Greek name: I am called the froth of nitre. Are you a Greek? Aphronitrum.'

poems.title: Book XIV, 59 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Balsams attract me; these are the unguents of men ': ye matrons, exhale the choice perfumes of Cosmus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 60: Bean-meal (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: 'Twill be a welcome gift, and one not without use to a wrinkled belly, if in broad daylight you go to Stephanus' bath.

poems.title: Book XIV, 61: A Horn Lantern (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Guide of your way am I carried, a lantern golden with fenced flame, and safe in my bosom is a small light.

poems.title: Book XIV, 62: A Lantern made of Bladder (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If I be not of horn, am I the dimmer? or does he that meets mc think me a bladder?

poems.title: Book XIV, 63: Pipe of Reed (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Why do you laugh at me, compact of wax and reed? The first pipe that was made was such as I.

poems.title: Book XIV, 64 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The drunken flautist bursts our ears with her bibulous cheeks; often she uses two pipes at once, often only one.

poems.title: Book XIV, 65 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If it happens your slave is not at hand, and you want to put on your house-shoes, your foot will itself be its own slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 66: A Bosom-hand (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: "With a bull's hide" you might well have braced up your bosom; for this skin stomacher of yours is too small for your breasts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 67 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This which forbids foul flies to taste your meal was the proud tail of a peerless bird.

poems.title: Book XIV, 68 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Don't strike with your fist the teeth of your offending servant; let him eat the biscuit illustrious Rhodes has sent you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 69 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you want to satisfy your hunger you can eat my Priapus; you may gnaw his very appendage, yet you will be undefiled.

poems.title: Book XIV, 70: Pig (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This pig will make you a "Good Saturnalia ": he was fed on acorns among the foaming boars.

poems.title: Book XIV, 71 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If your dress has been soiled with yellow dust let this light ox-tail emend this with a gentle flap.

poems.title: Book XIV, 72: A Sausage (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The sausage that has reached you at the mid-season of winter had reached me before Saturn's seven days."

poems.title: Book XIV, 73 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I, A PARROT, will learn of you the names of others: this I learned of my own accord to say, "Caesar, hail!"

poems.title: Book XIV, 75 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Philomela laments the crime of incestuous Tereus: she who was a silent maiden is acclaimed as a bird of song.

poems.title: Book XIV, 76: Magpie (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A chattering pie, I with intelligible voice salute you, my master; did you not see me you -will say I am no bird.

poems.title: Book XIV, 77 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you shall have such a bird as Lesbia, beloved of Catullus, mourned, here it can dwell.

poems.title: Book XIV, 78 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You see a medicine chest, the ivory equipment of a doctor's art: you will have a gift which Paccius would wish his own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 79 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Play, ye jovial slaves, but play only; I will keep these sealed up for five days.

poems.title: Book XIV, 80 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Hated much by boys and welcome to school-masters, we are the wood made famous by Prometheus' gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 81: Wallet (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That he may not carry the mendicant scraps of a half-clad bearded philosopher, nor sleep with a sour cynic, is the prayer of the wallet.

poems.title: Book XIV, 82 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The palm-tree testifies that brooms were once in demand, but the crumb-collector has now given a rest to brooms.

poems.title: Book XIV, 83 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This hand will protect your shoulder-blades when "an irritating flea is biting you, or any insect fouler than a flea.

poems.title: Book XIV, 84 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: To prevent your toga or cloak making your books frayed, this fir-wood will give long life to your paper.

poems.title: Book XIV, 85 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The bird, most lovely with its painted plumage, gives its name to a couch; it is now the bird of Juno, but once it was Argus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 86 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Take, hunter, the housing of a nimble steed, for from a bare-backed horse piles are wont to spring.

poems.title: Book XIV, 87 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Rf.ceive a horse-shoe couch inlaid with crescent lines of tortoise-shell. It takes eight: let everyone come who shall be my friend.

poems.title: Book XIV, 88 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you think shell of a female land-tortoise is part of me, you are deceived: I am the male catch of the sea.

poems.title: Book XIV, 89 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive this wood of a fruitful tree, the offering of Atlas: he who shall give you golden gifts will give you less.

poems.title: Book XIV, 90 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I am indeed not veined, nor the daughter of a Moorish forest, but even my wood knows sumptuous feasts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 91 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Tusks that upbear the huge bodies of bulls ® — do you ask whether they can uphold tables of Libyan wood?

poems.title: Book XIV, 92: Five-foot Rule (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: An oaken rule, marked off into lengths and ending in a sharp point, is often apt to detect a contractor's fraud.

poems.title: Book XIV, 93: Antique Cups (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That is no recent work, nor pride of Roman chisel; Mentor made these cups and first drank from them.

poems.title: Book XIV, 94 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We are plebeian chased cups of dreadnought glass, and our ware is not cracked by boiling water.

poems.title: Book XIV, 95: Chased Gold Bowl (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Though I am noble and ruddy with Gallician ore, I gloiy more in my workmanship, for of Mys was the labour you see.

poems.title: Book XIV, 96 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive a cup, a cheap memento of cobbler Vatinius, but that nose was longer.

poems.title: Book XIV, 97: Gold-inlaid Dishes (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Do not insult large gold-inlaid dishes with a small mullet: at the least it ought to weigh two pounds.

poems.title: Book XIV, 98 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We advise you not overmuch to despise Arretian vases: Tuscan earthenware was luxury to Porsena.

poems.title: Book XIV, 99: Basket (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I have come, a barbarian basket, from the woad-stained Britons; but Rome now prefers to call me her own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 100 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If the country of the elegant Catullus is not unknown to you, you have drunk Rhaetian wine from my crock.

poems.title: Book XIV, 101 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although mushrooms have given me so noble a name, yet I am a slave — alas! I am ashamed to own it — to early greens.

poems.title: Book XIV, 102 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive chalices not sprung of common clay, out the smooth embossed work of a Surrentine potter's-wheel.

poems.title: Book XIV, 103 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: With the snow I contain, I warn you, subdue your cups of Setine: in a poorer wine you may dip linen bags.

poems.title: Book XIV, 104 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: My linen also knows how to liquefy snow: no colder spirts the water from your strainer.

poems.title: Book XIV, 105: Small Jugs for -Table-service (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Cold water will not be wanting; there will not be wanting hot, if you ask for it; but do not you be dainty with a craving thirst.

poems.title: Book XIV, 106 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Here is given you a red jug with a spreading handle: Stoic Fronto used to go to this for cold water.

poems.title: Book XIV, 107 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The Satyrs love us, Bacchus loves us; us, too, the drunken tigress which has been taught to lick the wine-dabbled feet of her master.

poems.title: Book XIV, 108 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Take cups made of Saguntine clay, which without anxiety your servant may handle and guard.

poems.title: Book XIV, 109 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: See how the gold gleams, gemmed with the fire of Scythian emeralds! How many fingers has that chalice stripped!

poems.title: Book XIV, 110 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In this jewelled flask that bears the name of Cosmus you may drink, luxurious man, if your thirst is for perfumed wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 111: Crystal Cups (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: So long as you fear to break them, you will break crystal cups: hands too careless and too anxious alike offend.

poems.title: Book XIV, 112 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The storm-cloud that comes from Jove will pour you water in plenty to blend your cups: this one will give you wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 113 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you drink your wine warm, murrine suits the burning Falernian, and better flavour comes therefrom to the wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 114 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This platter, her own townsman, ruddy with the soil of. Cumae, the chaste Sibyl has sent you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 115: Glass Chalices (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You observe the ingenuity of Egypt. Ah, how often has the artist, in wisliing to make additions, ruined his work!

poems.title: Book XIV, 116 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You drink Spoletine, or wine stored in Marsian cellars: what is the use to you of the noble coolness of boiled water?

poems.title: Book XIV, 117: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The drinking, not of snow, but of water fresh from the snow, the ingenuity of thirst has devised.

poems.title: Book XIV, 118 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Boy, forbear to mix Massilia's smoke with iced water, that the water may not cost you more than the wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 119 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: While I am called for by a snapping of the fingers,® and the home-born slave lingers, oh, how often has a pillow been made my rival!

poems.title: Book XIV, 120 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: However much both knights and senators may call me ligula, I am called by ignorant grammarians lingula.

poems.title: Book XIV, 121: A Snail-pick (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I am convenient for eating snails, and no less useful for eating eggs. Do you know why I am rather called a snail-pick?

poems.title: Book XIV, 122: Rings (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Formerly many a friend gave us as presents, but now here and there a friend. Happy is he whose, comrade is a knight he himself has made '&

poems.title: Book XIV, 123 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Often a heavy ring slips from fingers moist with unguent; but your gem will be made safe in my faithful charge.

poems.title: Book XIV, 124: Toga (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: He makes the Romans "lords of the world and the race that wears the toga," who granted his mighty sire immortality.

poems.title: Book XIV, 125: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If it comes easily to you to lose your morning sleep, by wearing out your toga a dole will often come to you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 126 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: 'Tis a poor man's offering but not a poor man's wear. This wrapper I send you in place of a cloak.

poems.title: Book XIV, 127 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This cloak of Canusian wool, very like in colour to turbid mead, shall be your present. Rejoice: it will not quickly become old.

poems.title: Book XIV, 128 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Gaul clothes you in a Santonian cowled cloak. Formerly it was the frock of long-tailed monkeys.

poems.title: Book XIV, 129 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Rome is clad more in brown, Gaul in red, and this colour pleases boys and soldiers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 130 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Although you may set out on your journey when the sky is continuously serene, let a leather surtout nowhere be wanting against sudden showers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 131: Scarlet Mantle (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you favour the Blue or the Green, why will you assume scarlet? See that by this lot you do not become a deserter,

poems.title: Book XIV, 132: Cap (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If I could, I should have wished to have sent a mantle complete: now I send you a present only for your head.

poems.title: Book XIV, 133 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: My wool is not deceptive, nor am I transformed in the vat. Let Tyrian mantles please you by such means: my own sheep dyed me.

poems.title: Book XIV, 134 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Stomacher, compress the swelling breasts of my mistress that there may be something for my hand to seize and cover.

poems.title: Book XIV, 136 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In the winter season smooth coverings do not much avail: my wool makes warm your outer garment.

poems.title: Book XIV, 137: White Mantles (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: We recommend ourselves by our use in the amphitheatre, when a white mantle shall cover a chilly toga.

poems.title: Book XIV, 138 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let woollen cloths cover your nobler citrus wood: on my round tables a circular mark may stand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 139 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: CXXXIX,— Libumian Hood You have not known, O foolish fellow, how to match your mantle with me: you put it on white; take it off now green.

poems.title: Book XIV, 140 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Wool did not supply these, but the beard of the noisome husband: your foot will be able to take refuge in a Cinyphian nest.

poems.title: Book XIV, 141 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: While the toga gladly rests for five days, you may assume this garb as of right.

poems.title: Book XIV, 142 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Iv, meaning to recite, I shall perhaps have sent you a note of invitation, let this comforter emancipate your ears.

poems.title: Book XIV, 143 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Paduan garments of triple thread use up many fleeceSj and only a saw can sever the thick tunics.

poems.title: Book XIV, 144: A Sponge (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This sponge is given you by lot: it is useful for wiping tables when it lightly swells after the water has been squeezed out.

poems.title: Book XIV, 145 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Such is my whiteness, the beauty of my wool is such, that you would choose to wear me even in the midst of harvest.

poems.title: Book XIV, 146: Pillow (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Anoint your head with Cosmus' unguent, your pillow will smell of it: when your hair has lost the fragrance the feathers retain it.

poems.title: Book XIV, 147 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Your coverlet of wool is bright with purple bro-cade. What is the use of it if an aged wife freeze you .''

poems.title: Book XIV, 148 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: That the sacking on your bare bed might not show, we sisters, knit together, have come to you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 149 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I shrink from big-breasted women: hand me over to some young girl, that my linen may enjoy a bosom of snow.

poems.title: Book XIV, 150 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This present the land of Memphis makes you: now has the needle of Babylon been surpassed by the sley of the Nile.

poems.title: Book XIV, 151: A Female Girdle (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Long enough am I now; but if your shape should swell under its grateful burden, then shall I become to you a narrow girdle.

poems.title: Book XIV, 152 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Blankets the country of elegant Catullus will send you: we are from the region of Helicaon.

poems.title: Book XIV, 153 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let a rich man give a tunic: I can gird you in front. Were I rich, I would give both gifts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 154 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Drunken as I am with the blood of Sidon's shell-fish, I do not see why I am called sober wool.''

poems.title: Book XIV, 155: White Wool (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Apulia is renowned for the finest wool/ Parma for second quality; its sheep, third in rank, commend Altinum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 156: Tyrian Wools (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Us the shepherd gave to his Lacedaemonian mistress i of less worth was the purple of her mother Leda.

poems.title: Book XIV, 157 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This land is wont to supply not only wool that mourns with its black fleece: it supplies also its native chalices.

poems.title: Book XIV, 158: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: My wool is indeed sad in hue, but 'tis fit for closeclipt attendants, such as — but not from the first rank of slaves — the table summons.

poems.title: Book XIV, 159 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Is the bed-girth "too near the feather pillow you crush down. Accept fleeces shorn for Leuconian cloaks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 160 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Marsh-reed chopped up is called Circensian stuffing. This litter the poor man buys in lieu of Leuconian.

poems.title: Book XIV, 161: Feathers (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Tired you may rest on feathers of Amyclae which the swan's inner down has given you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 162 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: I.ET your rustling mattress swell with thefts from your mule: pale Care comes not to hard couches.

poems.title: Book XIV, 163 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Give up the ball: the bell of the warm baths is sounding. Do you go on playing .'' You want to go home after a bath in the Virgin water only.

poems.title: Book XIV, 164 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: While the burnished weight of the Spartan quoit is flying, keep far off, ye boys: let that quoit be guilty only once.

poems.title: Book XIV, 165 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: It restored Eurydice to her bard; but he himself lost her, trusting not himself, nor loving with patience.

poems.title: Book XIV, 166: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Often has that been driven from Pompey's theatre, which drew after it woods and stayed wild beasts. CLXVIL— Quill for Playing the Lyre That an angry blister may not arise on your chafed thumb, let an ivory quill embellish your responsive lyre.

poems.title: Book XIV, 168: Hoop (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The wheel must be fitted with a tyre: you give me a useful present; this to boys will be a hoop, but to me a tyre.

poems.title: Book XIV, 169: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Why do noisy rings wander round the wide orbit? That the crowd that meets them may give way to tinkling hoops.

poems.title: Book XIV, 170: Golden Statue of Victory (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: She is given without a drawn lot to him to whom Rhine has given a true victor's name. Ten times pour Falernian, boy.

poems.title: Book XIV, 171 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The renown of so small a statue is not unknown. Of this boy was Brutus the lover.

poems.title: Book XIV, 178: J Hercules in Clay (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Fragile am I, but do not you, I charge you, despise my small statue: it shames not Alcides to bear my name.

poems.title: Book XIV, 179: A Minerva in Silver (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Tell me, gallant maid, whereas thou hast thy helm and thy spear why hast thou not thine aegis? "Caesar has it."

poems.title: Book XIV, 180 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Better, most excellent Father of the Gods, couldst thou have been changed into a bull when lo was to thee a heifer.'

poems.title: Book XIV, 181: Marble Leander (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Daring Leander cried amid the swelling waters: "Drown me, ye waves, when I am turning home."

poems.title: Book XIV, 182 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: 'TvvAS a drunken Prometheus, I fancy, made for the earth this monster; he himself, too, played viith Saturnalian clay. CLXXXIIL— //07ner' "Battle of Frogs and Mice"

poems.title: Book XIV, 183 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Read through the story of the frogs sung in Homer's lay, and learn to smooth your brow by means of my trifles.

poems.title: Book XIV, 184 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The Iliad and the tale of Ulysses, foe to Priam's realm, both lie stored in many-folded skins.

poems.title: Book XIV, 185: Virgil's Gnat (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Receive, studious reader, the Gnat of eloquent Maro; you need not then lay aside your nuts to read "Arms and the Man."

poems.title: Book XIV, 186 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: How short a parchment has comprised the mighty Maro! The features of the man himself the first leaf beai-s.

poems.title: Book XIV, 187 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: With this first he lightly touched youth's wanton love, and Glycera was not the mistress of his boyhood: 'twas Thais.

poems.title: Book XIV, 188: Cicero in Parchment (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If this parchment shall be your travelling companion, imagine you are taking a long journey with Cicero.

poems.title: Book XIV, 189 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Cynthia, the theme of eloquent Propertius' youthful song, won from him fame; no less she herself bestowed.

poems.title: Book XIV, 190 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Narrowed into scanty skins is bulky Livy, the whole of whom my library does not contain.

poems.title: Book XIV, 191 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Here will be Crispus, first of Roman historians, as the judgment of learned men declares.

poems.title: Book XIV, 192 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This bulk, that has been formed of many a leaf, contains the fifteen books of Naso's poems.

poems.title: Book XIV, 193 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Wanton Nemesis fired her lover Tibullus, whom it pleased to be "of no account in his own house."

poems.title: Book XIV, 194 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Some are there that say I am no poet: but the bookseller that sells me thinks I am.

poems.title: Book XIV, 195: Catullus (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: As much great Verona owes to her Catullus as small Mantua owes to her Virgil.

poems.title: Book XIV, 196 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: These sheetSj that speak to you of fountains and of the names of rivers themselves will better swim in the waters they tell of.

poems.title: Book XIV, 197: Dwarf Mules (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: From these mules no fall is to be apprehended: you are used to sit almost higher on the ground.

poems.title: Book XIV, 198 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you wish to hear the tricks of a small lapdog, for the telling a whole page of mine is too short.

poems.title: Book XIV, 199 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This little horse, that picks up its hurrying hoof in measured time, has come from tribes rich in gold, an Asturian steed.

poems.title: Book XIV, 200 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Not for himself, but for his master, hunts the keen greyhound, who will bring you a hare unwounded by his tooth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 202 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A monkey cunning to avoid darts hurled at me, I should be a "long-tailed ape" had I a tail.

poems.title: Book XIV, 204 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: The brazen cymbals that mourn for the boy of Celaenae, the darling of the Great Mother, her priest is often wont to sell when hungry.

poems.title: Book XIV, 205: Young Slave (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: May I have a boy with a cheek smooth with youth, not with pumice, for whose sake no maid would please me.

poems.title: Book XIV, 206: Cestus (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Round thy neck twine, boy, love's very essence, a cestus warm from the bosom of Venus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 207: The Same (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Take thou the cestus imbued with Cytherea's nectar: this girdle fired the lover Jove.

poems.title: Book XIV, 208 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Albeit the words speedy the hand is swifter than they: not yet has the tongue, the hand has finished its work.

poems.title: Book XIV, 209: Sea-shell (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let the rind of the Mareotic rush be made smooth by the sea-shell: the reed-pen will run on an unimpeded path.

poems.title: Book XIV, 210: A Natural (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: His dulness is not assumed, or pretended by crafty art. He that has wits no more than is enough has his wits.

poems.title: Book XIV, 211: Rams Head (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: You have cut the soft throat of the lord of the flock, a ram of Phryxus; did he deserve this who gave you, cruel man, your tunic

poems.title: Book XIV, 212 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: If you regard the man's head alone you would believe him Hector; if you saw him standing you would deem him Astyanax.

poems.title: Book XIV, 213: Small Shield (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: This, which is wont oft to be overcome, rarely to win, will be to you a small buckler, but a dwarf's great shield.

poems.title: Book XIV, 214 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: In all tins troupe will be no one "Tlie Hated"; [but any one of them can be "The Double Deceiver."

poems.title: Book XIV, 215 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Tell me candidly, O clasp, what do you guarantee to comedians and harp-players } "The greater value of their favours."

poems.title: Book XIV, 216 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: He preyed once upon birds; the servant of the fowler now, he strikes them down, and is sad the birds are not taken for his own behoof.

poems.title: Book XIV, 217 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: CCXVIL— /f Caterer Say with how many and at what cost you want to dine, and do not add another word: your dinner is ready for you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 218 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Not only by canes, but by a bird's note also is the bird deceived while the cunning reed is being lengthened by the noiseless hand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 219 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Seeing that you, a poor lawyer, write poems thai do not bring you in a penny, take from me pluck like your own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 220: Cook (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Insufficient is his art alone for a cook: I would not have his palate that of a slave; a cook ought to possess the taste of his master.

poems.title: Book XIV, 221 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Let your grated gridiron be unctuous with the rounded cutlet; on the long pointed spit let a foaming boar smoke.

poems.title: Book XIV, 222 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: A thousand toothsome shapes of handiwork that hand will construct for you; for him alone labours the frugal bee.

poems.title: Book XIV, 223 (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Get up: already the baker is sellino-to boys their breakfast, and the crested fowls of dawn are crowing on all sides.

poems.title: Book XIV, 224: Epigram of Uncertain Position (Ker)
poems.author: Martial
poems.text: Flavian family, of how much glory has thy third heir robbed thee! Well nigh had it stood us in stead not to have possessed the twain!
